title: Food at College
text:
Background
The linkage of diet with weight management has drawn some interest in recent years, with the spiraling prevalence of obesity and related metabolic conditions in many parts of the world. Though there is documented evidence that what we consume greatly influences body weight, much about how changes in eating habits contribute differently toward weight is still highly elusive. While some reveal striking weight change with either an improvement or deterioration in diet, others seem to be unaffected by similar alterations. These observations raise the following questions: whether same, better, or worse eating behavioral changes-represent weight change uniformly across individuals.

title: Food at College
text:
Data
In this analysis we want to look at different people’s eating changes to know if each change equally affects a person’s weight or not. The different eating changes have been coded with ‘same’, ‘worse’ and ’better’The people in this analysis they were asked to honestly document what they feel about their eating changes and they had to select which of three opitions best suits them. Below is a data with the results of this questionaire

title: Food at College
text:
Analysis
From our sample we can graphically compare the weights and eating changes of our analysis participants to know what the common trend is in their weights with reference to their eating changes.

library(plotly)

plot_ly(new, y = ~weight, x = ~as.factor(eating_changes_coded), 
        color = ~as.factor(eating_changes_coded), 
        type = "box", 
        colors = "Set3") %>%
  layout(
    title = list(
      text = "Effects of new habits on a persons weight",
      x = 0.5,
      xanchor = "center",
      font = list(size = 18, color = 'rgb(34,34,34)')
    ),
    xaxis = list(
      title = "Different Eating Changes",
      titlefont = list(size = 14),
      tickfont = list(size = 12),
      tickangle = -45  # Rotate x-axis labels for readability
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      title = "Weight (lbs)",
      titlefont = list(size = 14),
      tickfont = list(size = 12)
    ),
    showlegend = FALSE
  )






new<-na.omit(new)
new <- new[-3, ]
new$weight<- as.numeric(new$weight)
new$eating_changes_coded <- as.factor(new$eating_changes_coded)
favstats(as.numeric(weight)~eating_changes_coded,main="mean of weights for the different eating changes",data=droplevels(new)) %>%
  pander(caption= "mean weight of each group", split.table=Inf)

Above we have the box plots with some numerical summary and a table of means for each group.From this data we see that the same group have on average people with the highest weight(174.6).Right after them is the better group(166.8) and then the worse(152.6). Looking at the box plot we can take the cursor to each box and it will display more information about that particular group, and we can use this to compare more data.
Now for the true purpose of this analysis we want to know if each eating change has the same effect on weight or if at least one has a different effect. And for us to do this we just need to know if all groups belong to the same sampling distribution. \[
H_0:\text{ (All eating change groups belong to the same sample distribution)}\\
\] \[
H_0:\text{ (At least one group is stochastically different than the others)}\\
\]
\[
α=0.05
\]

kruskal.test(weight~eating_changes_coded,data=new) %>% pander()

title: Food at College
text:
Conclusion
The results of the analysis shows that each of the different eating changes all have the same effect on a persons body weight, or even if the effects aren’t exactly the same the difference is too little to be considered.So if a person really wants to alter their body weights changing their eating habits wont be the only thing that will help them accomplish this.we were able to conclude this because from our analysis above we can see that the test had a p-value of 0.06115 and as compared to our significance level (0.05) we will fail to reject our null hypothesis because there is in sufficient evidence for the alternative. title: Chi Squared Test
text:
Background
Coffee is one of the most consumed beverages in the world, with many types to suit every person’s taste. Understanding preferences can give a clue to the marketers and the coffee shops on whom to target. This analysis will, therefore, seek to answer the following question: Is there a relationship between a person’s age and the type of coffee preferred-a person who prefers Espresso, Latte, Cappuccino, or Americano? In this relationship, we seek to understand if age impacts coffee preferences for the pursuit of appropriate advertising and tailoring of the menu items. For this analysis we got data from a coffee shop by asking the customers from the several age groups which one they preferred. Below is the table of the data collected

coffee <- data.frame(
  Age_Group = c("18-25", "26-35", "36-50", "51+"),
  Espresso = c(22, 25, 34, 19),
  Latte = c(30, 35, 28, 24),
  Cappuccino = c(28, 29, 31, 15),
  Americano = c(20, 18, 22, 27)
)
coffee_table <- as.table(t(as.matrix(coffee[, -1])))
rownames(coffee_table) <- coffee$Age_Group 
colnames(coffee_table) <- c("Espresso", "Latte", "Cappuccino", "Americano")

title: Chi Squared Test
text:
Analysis
For this analysis we are trying to know if age and coffee type are independent or associated and if they are associated what they exact correlation would be. We would now be conducting a hypothesis test to know if they are independent or not.
\[
H_0: \text{Age and coffee type are independent}.
\]
\[
H_0: \text{Age and coffee type are not independent(associated)}.
\]
\[
\alpha = 0.05
\]
For this test we use an alpha of 0.05 that allows us to know if we reject the null or not. Basically rejecting the null tells us age and coffee type are associated meanwhile accepting the null tells us they are not. We can also make use of graphical summaries to compare each coffee type and age visually.

coffee_data <- matrix(c(22, 30, 28, 20, 25, 35, 29, 18, 34, 28, 31, 22, 19, 24, 15, 27), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)
bp <- barplot(coffee_data, beside=TRUE, col=c("wheat", "navy", "darkgreen", "grey"),
              legend.text=c("Espresso", "Latte", "Cappuccino", "Americano"),
              args.legend = list(x="topright", bty="n", title="Coffee Type", cex=0.7),
              xlab="Age Group", main="Coffee Preferences of each Age Group",
              ylab="Frequency of coffee consumers")
age_groups <- c("18-25", "26-35", "36-50", "51+")
text(x=colMeans(bp), y=-1, labels=age_groups, srt=45, adj=1, xpd=TRUE)








From the graphs above we now have a basic idea of what type of coffee each age group would prefer.And we can solidfy this claim even better by running proper statistical analysis to back it up.

qs2Chi<-chisq.test(coffee_table)
pander(qs2Chi)

title: Chi Squared Test
text:
Intepretaion
From our analysis above we had a p-value of 0.2558 and failed to reject the Null and so that means that both age and coffee type are independent. Please note that this data only covered a very small population and doesn’t really reflect the actual results in reality. So with this it would be advised that more research and statistical analysis be carried out on this subject for more accurate information.
